methods: ARCH LM, Breusch-Pagan, Breusch-Godfrey, CUSUM diagnostics

Internal inconsistencies in Table 3: lnF coefficient 0.36091 reported with t = -2.81 and lnU -0.03481 with t = 3.95 (signs of coefficient and t-statistic disagree). Text says diagnostic results 'rejected all the respective null hypotheses' although p-values (0.39-0.95) indicate non-rejection (p.8). Unedited journal-template sentence left in Section 4.1 ('Authors should discuss the results...', p.6). CO2 is total EDGAR emissions; aviation/jet fuel is only discussed qualitatively (Dubai airport, p.8), not separately measured. Number of observations not reported. Granger causality: bidirectional between tourist arrivals and CO2 (Table 4, p.10).

setting: Saudi Arabia (single-country time series; pilgrimage/Hajj tourism)
data_source: CO2 emissions and energy consumption: BP Statistics; GDP (current US$): World Development Indicators; foreign pilgrims: Saudi General Authority for Statistics (Hajj statistics)
methods: ADF and Phillips-Perron unit root tests
LM serial correlation, Breusch-Pagan, Jarque-Bera residual tests

E.estimator: Johansen cointegration + Vector Error Correction Model (maximum likelihood), lag 2
tourism_variables: lnnp: number of foreign pilgrims' arrival (Hajj)

key_results.coefficient: 0.0719 (normalized cointegrating vector; paper states signs should be reversed)
key_results.evidence: number of foreign pilgrims' arrival has a negative and significant impact on lnc in the long run (p.282); Table 4: lnnp 0.0719 (0.000)
However, for every percentage point of foreign pilgrims' arrival, carbon emissions go up by 0.114% (p.282)

out_of_sample_forecast.evidence: Only Cholesky variance decomposition over periods 1-8 is reported (Table 6, p.283); no out-of-sample forecasting.

E1_unit_root_tests.evidence: According to the results, all the series contain unit roots at the level and become stationary when the first differences are taken (p.280, Table 1 ADF & PP)

E2_cointegration_or_long_run_test.evidence: the study concludes that there is a long run relationship between carbon emissions, energy consumption, economic growth and foreign pilgrims' arrival in Saudi Arabia (Johansen, Table 3, p.281)

E3_structural_breaks.evidence: No structural break tests or break dummies reported; tests listed are ADF, PP, Johansen, VECM, Granger, variance decomposition and residual tests (p.284).

E4_cross_sectional_dependence_or_heterog.evidence: using annual time series data from 1996 to 2022 (Abstract, p.273)

E5_endogeneity_or_omitted_variables_addr.evidence: Only energy consumption and GDP included as regressors, following Ozturk et al (2021): "econometric models used by Ozturk et al (2021) before" (p.279); no endogeneity discussion.

E6_diagnostics_stability.evidence: The tests return, in that order, p - values of 0.2168, 0.4378, and 0.70740 [serial correlation, heteroscedasticity, normality] (p.283, Table 7)

E7_data_source_and_period.evidence: Statistics on energy consumption and carbon dioxide emissions are from BP ... Saudi Arabia from 1996-2022 (p.278)

notes: Contradictory reporting of the tourism effect: long-run pilgrims coefficient described as negative ('Carbon emission is negatively correlated with number of pilgrims arrival'), short-run +0.114, abstract says pilgrims 'negatively affects carbon emissions' yet 'still contributes significantly to carbon emissions'; conclusion also says 'Pilgrimage tourism growth will drop by 0.07 percent as carbon dioxide levels rise'. Johansen interpretation is questionable (null said rejected when statistics are below critical values, p.281). Jarque-Bera H0 mis-stated as 'Residuals are not normally distributed' (Table 7). Conclusion mentions an impulse response function that is not reported. Short-run coefficient significance not reported. Short sample (1996-2022), n_obs not stated. CO2 measure from BP (energy-related); aviation emissions not separated.
